questions.question: What is Bayes' rule for events $A$ and $B$ with positive probabilities?
options: $P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)}$
$P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}$
$P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)P(B)}{P(A)}$
$P(A\mid B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)$

questions.question: How is Bayes' rule obtained?
options: By assuming that $A$ and $B$ are independent events
By setting $\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)$ equal to $\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)$ directly
By writing $\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)$ two ways via conditioning
By writing $\mathbb{P}(A\cup B)$ in two ways by inclusion-exclusion

questions.question: In a diagnostic-test setting, which probability is a posterior probability?
options: The probability of a positive test given disease
The unconditional prevalence alone
The number of possible test outcomes
The probability of disease given a positive test

questions.question: Why is Bayes' rule helpful when $P(B\mid A)$ is easier than $P(A\mid B)$?
options: It shows the two conditionals are equal, so either may be used
It converts the easier conditional into the reverse direction
It gives $P(A\mid B)$ from $P(B\mid A)$ alone, without any prior
It applies only when $A$ and $B$ are independent events

questions.question: If $P(B\mid A)=0.2$, $P(A)=0.4$, and $P(B)=0.5$, what is $P(A\mid B)$?
Why can a highly sensitive test still have low positive predictive value?
options: Most sick people test negative, so true positives are few
A rare disease lets false positives dominate positives
A common disease lets false positives outnumber true ones
The predictive value equals one minus the sensitivity

questions.question: Using the partition form, if $P(A_1)=0.2$, $P(A_2)=0.8$, $P(B\mid A_1)=0.9$, and $P(B\mid A_2)=0.1$, what is $P(A_1\mid B)$?

Let $A_1,A_2,A_3$ be a partition of a sample space $S$ with $\mathbb{P}(A_j)>0$ for each $j$, and let $B$ be an event with $0<\mathbb{P}(B)<1$. Which quantity equals $1$ for every such partition and event $B$?
options: $\mathbb{P}(B\mid A_1)+\mathbb{P}(B\mid A_2)+\mathbb{P}(B\mid A_3)$
$\mathbb{P}(A_1\mid B)+\mathbb{P}(A_1\mid B^c)$
$\mathbb{P}(B\mid A_1)\mathbb{P}(A_1)+\mathbb{P}(B\mid A_2)\mathbb{P}(A_2)+\mathbb{P}(B\mid A_3)\mathbb{P}(A_3)$
$\mathbb{P}(A_1\mid B)+\mathbb{P}(A_2\mid B)+\mathbb{P}(A_3\mid B)$

questions.question: A disease affects $2\%$ of a population. A screening test is positive for $95\%$ of people who have the disease and for $10\%$ of people who do not. A randomly chosen person tests positive. Approximately what is the probability that this person has the disease?

A disease affects $10\%$ of a population. A test is positive for $80\%$ of people who have the disease and for $10\%$ of people who do not. A randomly chosen person tests negative. Approximately what is the probability that this person has the disease?

A disease affects $20\%$ of a population. A test is positive for $90\%$ of people who have the disease and for $30\%$ of people who do not. A person takes the test twice, and given the disease status the two results are independent. Both results are positive. Approximately what is the probability that the person has the disease?

Three suppliers $A$, $B$ and $C$ deliver $50\%$, $35\%$ and $15\%$ of a factory's components. Their components are defective with probabilities $0.01$, $0.03$ and $0.05$, respectively. A randomly chosen component is defective. From which supplier did it most likely come?
options: Supplier $A$, as it has the largest share
Supplier $B$, as its share times defect rate is largest
Supplier $C$, as it has the largest defect rate
None can be named before $\mathbb{P}(\text{defective})$ is known

questions.question: A disease affects $1\%$ of a population. A test is positive for $90\%$ of people who have the disease and is never positive for people who do not have it. A randomly chosen person tests positive. What is the probability that this person has the disease?
Events $A$ and $B$ satisfy $\mathbb{P}(A)=0.2$ and $\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)=\mathbb{P}(B\mid A^c)=0.3$. What is $\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)$?
